segments.text: On the internet, you can find timeshares for sale for one dollar. Some owners will even pay the closing costs, just to get rid of them.
And yet in 2025, Americans bought ten point seven billion dollars of brand-new timeshares, at an average of almost twenty-five thousand dollars each.
So why would anyone pay twenty-five thousand dollars for something that's worth almost nothing the moment they sign?
And how did one man selling them build the biggest house in America?
In 1980, David Siegel owned an orange grove near Orlando. One day, a man offered to buy part of it.

David Siegel, Westgate founder — "I said, what are you going to do with it? He says, I'm going to timeshare it. I said, what's that? He explained the concept to me. I fell in love with the concept. I didn't sell him the property. I decided I'm going to do it myself." | Fox Business, 2017
He built sixteen villas at the back of the grove. That became Westgate Resorts, which grew into one of the biggest timeshare companies in the world.
In 2004, he and his wife Jackie started building a house. Ninety thousand square feet. Modelled on the palace of Versailles.
Jackie Siegel — "It just became the largest home in America. We weren't trying to build the largest home in America. It just happened." | Fox Business, 2017
When the 2008 crash came, construction stopped. Credit dried up, timeshare sales collapsed, and Westgate cut jobs.
ABC News / David Siegel — "Her husband is 77-year-old billionaire David Siegel." / "I don't believe in wasting money." | ABC Good Morning America, Jul 2012

segments.cue: [DOC: CNN Money, Oct 2012: Siegel's email to employees]
segments.text: In 2012, Siegel emailed his seven thousand employees, warning that new taxes could force him to cut jobs if Barack Obama were re-elected. The email went viral.
Then the business came back. And so did the house.
So how does selling one week a year in Orlando pay for a palace?
It starts with a free gift. Show tickets. A cheap hotel stay. A cruise. All you have to do is sit through a ninety-minute presentation.

segments.cue: [GFX: "Hilton Grand Vacations, 2025: 856,676 tours · $3,851 sold per tour, on average"]
segments.text: The companies call it a tour, and they count them. In 2025, Hilton Grand Vacations ran over eight hundred and fifty thousand of them. On average, every tour brought in three thousand eight hundred and fifty-one dollars of sales.
That's why the free gift is worth it. And why ninety minutes can turn into something else. In 2015, a couple on holiday in Mexico told a San Francisco TV station what happened to them.

KPIX reporter / Susie High, timeshare buyer — "That 90 minutes they say turned into eight excruciating hours of rotating and relentless salespeople pressuring them." / "They kept pushing us and pushing us and we'd say no and they'd say something else." | KPIX 5 News, 24 Apr 2015
It's why many US states give timeshare buyers a few days to cancel, by law. In Florida, it's ten. Most people never use it.
Here's what the companies' own accounts show. In 2025, Marriott Vacations sold about one point eight billion dollars of timeshares.
It spent nine hundred and forty-three million on marketing and selling them.
About half.

segments.cue: [GFX: "Of every $1 you pay: ~52¢ to sell it to you"]
segments.text: So of every dollar a buyer pays, about fifty cents pays for the free gifts, the tours, the sales floor and the commissions. Only what's left pays for the holiday and the profit.
Which is why you can't give it away. The day you sign, you're holding half a product. The next buyer won't pay for the free gift you got.
World Property Channel guest, NBC Today — "You typically are making 20 cents on a dollar if you're lucky to sell it." | NBC Today, 23 May 2011
But the sale is only the beginning. Most buyers don't pay twenty-five thousand dollars in cash. The company lends it to them.

segments.cue: [GFX: "Hilton Grand Vacations: timeshare loans average 14.5% interest"]
segments.text: At Hilton Grand Vacations, those loans charge an average of fourteen and a half percent.
Here's an average timeshare, with simple numbers.
Twenty-four thousand seven hundred and forty dollars, borrowed at fourteen and a half percent over ten years, is about three hundred and ninety-two dollars a month.
By the end, you've paid about forty-seven thousand dollars.

segments.cue: [GFX: "Travel + Leisure: 20.7% of sales set aside for loans that won't be repaid"]
segments.text: The companies know many buyers won't make it. Travel + Leisure, one of the biggest timeshare sellers, sets aside about twenty-one cents of every dollar it sells, for loans it expects never to collect.
And when a buyer stops paying, the company can take the week back, and sell it again, to the next family on a free trip.
Then there's the part that never ends. Every timeshare comes with a yearly maintenance fee. In 2023, the average was twelve hundred and sixty dollars. By 2025, it was fifteen hundred and fifty.

segments.cue: [GFX: "Ten years: ~$47,000 loan + $15,500+ fees ≈ $62,500 for ten one-week holidays"]
segments.text: Add ten years of fees to the loan, and our average buyer has paid around sixty-two thousand dollars for ten weeks of holiday. About six thousand dollars a week.
And the fee keeps coming after the loan is paid off. Owners who want out often can't find anyone to take it.
Gary, timeshare owner — "Anybody even came in and said, I'll give you 50 cents, I would have said it's yours." | KPIX 5 News, Jul 2017

segments.cue: [DOC: California real estate commissioner warning on timeshare exit companies]
segments.text: That desperation has created a second industry: exit companies that promise to get owners out, for an upfront fee. Regulators warn many of them take the money and do nothing.
So why can't you give a timeshare away?

segments.cue: [GFX: the money: "Sale ~50% → selling it · loan 14.5% · fee forever"]
segments.text: Because you were never buying a holiday. About half of what you paid went on selling it to you. The company then lent you the rest at fourteen and a half percent, and charges you a fee that rises every year, for as long as you own it.
David Siegel died in April 2025, aged eighty-nine. The palace he started in 2004 was nearly finished.
He built it on a simple discovery from an orange grove in 1980: the holiday isn't the product. The sale is.
If you'll never sit through a free presentation the same way again, that's what this channel does: the economics nobody explains, one company at a time. Subscribe, and you'll get the next one.
